answer: I'd like to talk about some advice I gave to one of my oldest friends from university. A time I gave advice that actually made a difference was when this close friend was agonising over whether to change careers. He had been working in a bank for two years and was deeply unhappy in his job, because what he really wanted was to teach, but he was terrified of the [[uncertainty]] of starting over. He came to me feeling completely stuck, and I could see he just needed someone to help him think clearly. We met at our usual tea stall by the river and talked for hours. Rather than telling him what to do, I encouraged him to [[weigh up]] what he truly valued in the long term. I shared my own experience of taking a similar risk when I chose my current job, which seemed to [[reassure]] him. I also suggested he speak to a few teachers first, to see what the job was really like day to day. My main advice was that regret over never trying is usually worse than the fear of failing. It was a genuinely [[delicate]] conversation, because I did not want to push him into anything. In the end, he made the change and is now far happier teaching at a college. He told me recently that our conversation was the push he needed. Honestly, seeing him thrive was incredibly [[gratifying]], and it reminded me that sometimes the best help is simply helping someone find their own answer.

followUps.q: Do people often come to you for advice?
followUps.answer: Quite often, actually, probably because of my job. Students and their parents ask me about studying abroad every day, and friends seem to assume I am good with big decisions too.

followUps.q: Is there anyone whose advice you always trust?
followUps.answer: My grandfather. He is in his eighties but still remarkably sharp, and he has a way of cutting through a problem with one simple question. I always come away seeing things more clearly.

note: Friend from university moving from banking to teaching; talk by the river; linked to his own job choice; marked 'weigh up'.
